notes.34:16: The Greek reads "I will guard the strong" (to ischyron phylaxo), contrasting with the Masoretic Hebrew "the fat and the strong I will destroy."
notes.34:25: The Greek specifies "with David" (to Dauid) rather than "with them" as in the Masoretic Hebrew; similarly in 34:29 the Greek reads "a plant of peace" (phyton eirenes) rather than "a planting of renown."
notes.35:5: The Greek reads "you lay in ambush for the house of Israel with deceit, by the hand of enemies with the sword," where the Masoretic Hebrew speaks of giving over the sons of Israel to the power of the sword.
notes.35:6: The Greek preserves a shorter oath, "surely you have sinned even to blood, and blood shall pursue you," differing from the longer Masoretic Hebrew wording about preparing Mount Seir for blood.
notes.35:7: The Greek reads "men and beasts" (anthropous kai ktene) where the Masoretic Hebrew reads "the one who passes out and the one who returns."
notes.35:15: "Idumea" (Idoumaia) is the Greek proper name for Edom. The Greek verse is shorter than the Masoretic Hebrew and concludes with "the Lord their God."
notes.36:2: The Greek reads kyrios Kyrios (literally "lord Lord"), rendered "the Sovereign Lord" to distinguish it from simple Kyrios ("the Lord"). The Septuagint also reads "eternal wastes" (erema aionia), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "ancient heights."
notes.36:8: The Septuagint reads "your grapes" (ten staphylen) and "they are hoping to come" (elpizousin tou elthein), differing from the Hebrew "your branches" and "they are near to come."
notes.36:31: The Greek text employs third-person pronouns (auton, "their") in "before them" and "for their abominations," preserved faithfully here from the Septuagint.
notes.36:33: Here and in verse 37 the Greek transliterates Hebrew Adonai as adonai Kyrios ("Adonai, the Lord") rather than rendering it as kyrios Kyrios. In verse 35, "garden of delight" (kepos tryphes) translates the Hebrew name Eden.
notes.37:1: The Septuagint renders the setting as a "plain" (pediou) and explicitly specifies "human bones" (osteon anthropinon).
notes.37:9: Greek pneuma encompasses "spirit," "breath," and "wind" throughout verses 1-14; here the singular is rendered "the spirit" and the plural "the four winds." The Greek also reads "these dead ones" (tous nekrous toutous) rather than the Hebrew "these slain."
notes.37:19: Following the Septuagint, this verse reads "tribe" (phylen) for Joseph and Judah and "in the hand of Judah" (te cheiri Iouda), where the Hebrew reads "stick" and "in My hand."
notes.37:24: Here and in verses 22 and 25, the Septuagint uses "ruler" (archon) rather than "king," and places David "in their midst" (en meso auton).
notes.38:3: The Greek reads kyrios Kyrios ("the Lord, the Lord"), a doubled divine title characteristic of Septuagint Ezekiel, rendered literally throughout chapters 38-39.
notes.38:7: The Greek reads "a guard for Me" (moi), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "a guard for them."
notes.38:11: The Greek describes the land as "a cast-off land" (gen aperrimmenen), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("a land of unwalled villages").
notes.38:13: The Greek reads "Carthaginian merchants and all their villages," reflecting the Septuagint's identification of Tarshish with Carthage and reading "villages" where the Hebrew reads "young lions."
notes.39:6: The Greek reads "upon Gog, and the islands shall be inhabited in peace," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("upon Magog and on those who dwell securely in the coastlands").
notes.39:12: The Greek reads To te ("Te"), a textual form of To gai ("Gai," transliterating Hebrew gay, "valley"), which appears in verse 15; polyandrion denotes a common burial ground for a multitude.
notes.39:16: Polyandrion ("Burial Ground of a Multitude") is the Septuagint's Greek city name corresponding to Hebrew Hamonah.
notes.39:28: The Greek reads "when I appear to them among the nations," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to sending Israel into exile and gathering them back.
notes.39:29: The Greek reads "I have poured out My fury" (ton thymon mou) upon the house of Israel, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "My Spirit."
notes.40:6: Throughout chapter 40, the Greek text retains transliterated Hebrew architectural terms (ailam, thee/theim, thaielatha, aileu, ailammon, and ail), which are rendered here as vestibule(s), side chamber(s), and post(s) for clarity. Here the Greek also specifies seven steps, where the Hebrew does not give a number.
notes.40:17: The Greek reads "the inner court" here (and again in verse 34), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the outer court," and renders the surrounding structure as "colonnades" (peristyla) rather than a stone pavement.
notes.40:31: Verse 30 is absent from the Greek text, with verse 31 continuing directly from the measurements of verse 29.
notes.40:38: Verses 38–40 follow the shorter Greek text, which describes a "drain" (ekrysis) at the second gate, a "channel" (rhoax) of the burnt offerings, and sacrifices "for sin and for ignorance."
notes.40:43: The Greek describes a hewn rim of one handbreadth and "coverings" (stegas) over the tables to shelter them from rain and drought, differing notably from the Hebrew Masoretic Text; verses 48–49 likewise preserve the Greek measurements of fourteen cubits, twelve cubits, and ten steps.
notes.41:4: The Greek reads "the length of the doors, forty cubits," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "its length, twenty cubits."
notes.41:6: The Greek literally reads "thirty, three times, twice" and adds "for those who take hold to see" regarding the recessed space in the wall supporting the side chambers.
notes.41:8: "Thrael" renders the untranslated Greek transliteration thrael, denoting an architectural elevation around the house where the Hebrew reads "I saw."
notes.41:22: The Greek reads literally "before the face" (here "before the presence") without "of the Lord," explicitly specifies the breadth as two cubits, and reads "horns" and "base" where the Hebrew reads "corners" and "length."
notes.42:1: The Septuagint reads "into the inner court" (Hebrew: "outer court") and specifies "five chambers" (Hebrew: singular "the chamber").
notes.42:7: "Light" translates Greek phos, used throughout verses 7 through 12 (and 41:11) for an architectural opening or lighted space where the Hebrew reads "wall" or "front."
notes.42:13: The Septuagint explicitly identifies the ministering priests as "the sons of Zadok" and renders the guilt offerings as "the offerings for ignorance."
notes.42:16: In verses 16 through 20, the Greek measures the outer perimeter as five hundred cubits on each side (explicitly "cubits" in verses 17 and 20) rather than five hundred reeds as in the Hebrew, and in verse 20 refers to "the outer wall" rather than "the common."
notes.43:2: The Septuagint reads "the sound of the camp was like the sound of many redoubling their voices," contrasting with the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "like the sound of many waters."
notes.43:3: The Septuagint reads "to anoint the city" rather than "to destroy the city" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, and explicitly adds "of the chariot" in describing the vision.
notes.43:14: The Septuagint renders the altar ledges as "propitiatory" (the same term used for the mercy seat in Exodus) and reads "this great propitiatory beneath" in the first clause before referring to "the small propitiatory" in the second.
notes.43:15: "Ariel" preserves the Septuagint transliteration for the altar hearth, and the Greek text reads "and above the horns is a cubit" rather than specifying four horns.
notes.43:26: "Fill their hands" translates the literal Septuagint idiom signifying priestly consecration and ordination.
notes.44:2: The Septuagint uses the future tense "shall enter through it," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text uses the past tense "has entered."
notes.44:8: The Septuagint preserves a shorter text than the Hebrew Masoretic Text, omitting the opening clause about failing to keep charge of the holy things.
notes.44:18: The Septuagint reads "gird themselves tightly" (literally "with force"), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to girding with anything that causes sweat.
notes.44:20: Instead of prohibiting long hair and commanding trimming as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, the Septuagint forbids stripping the hair bare and commands that the priests "surely cover their heads."
notes.45:1: The Greek text specifies a width of twenty thousand (also in verses 3 and 5), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads ten thousand.
notes.45:12: The Greek defines the mina as fifty shekels (using Greek weights and measures such as obols, choenix, gomor, and kotyles in verses 10-14), whereas the Masoretic Text totals sixty shekels; similarly, verse 15 specifies one sheep out of ten rather than two hundred.
notes.45:20: The Greek dates this rite to the first day of the seventh month with a portion from each person, whereas the Masoretic Text specifies the seventh day of the first month for anyone who errs or is simple.
notes.45:25: "Grain offering" translates Greek manaa (here and in 46:5, 7, 11, 14, 15, 20), a transliteration of Hebrew minchah.
notes.46:2: "Porch" translates Greek ailam (also in 46:8), a transliteration of Hebrew ulam; the Greek also reads "the inner gate" rather than "from outside."
notes.46:20: "Offerings for ignorance" faithfully renders Greek agnoias, the Septuagint equivalent here for the Hebrew guilt offering.
notes.46:22: "Small court" preserves the Septuagint rendering of a difficult Hebrew architectural term often translated "unenclosed" or "vaulted."
notes.47:3: "Water of release" renders Greek hydor apheseos (which can also refer to a water channel or discharge), where the Masoretic Text reads "ankle-deep water"; in verse 4 the Greek likewise reads "thighs" rather than "knees."
notes.47:8: The Greek renders the Hebrew geographical terms gelilah ("region") and Arabah as the proper names "Galilee" and "Arabia."
notes.47:12: "Nothing upon it shall grow old" and "their growth" (anabasis) follow the Greek text closely where the Masoretic Text explicitly mentions leaves.
notes.47:13: "An addition of a measuring line" reflects the Greek etymological rendering of the Hebrew name Joseph as "addition" (prosthesis).
notes.47:15: Several place names in verses 15-19 preserve distinctive Septuagint forms (Hema, Seldamma, Abthera, Sebram, Heliam, court of Saunan, Hauranitis, Loranitis, Gileaditis, Phoenicon, Teman, and Marimoth Kadem) that differ from the Masoretic Text.
notes.47:22: The Greek reads "they shall eat" (phagontai) where the Masoretic Text has "they shall fall [by lot]," and in verse 23 reads "in the tribe of the proselytes, among the proselytes who are with them."
notes.48:1: The Greek renders the northern landmarks as "the descent of that which divides" (where Hebrew has "the way of Hethlon") and "the court of Ailam" (where Hebrew has Hazar-enan).
notes.48:9: The Greek text gives a width of twenty-five thousand here and a total width of twenty thousand in verse 13, while verse 10 omits the eastern side and reads "the mountain of the holy things" where Hebrew has "the sanctuary of the Lord."
notes.48:15: The Greek renders the Hebrew term for common land as "outer rampart" (proteichisma).
notes.48:28: The Greek reads "Teman" (for Hebrew Tamar), the distinct place name "Barimoth Kadesh" (for Meribath-kadesh), and "of the inheritance" (reading Hebrew nahalah as "inheritance" rather than "to the brook").
notes.48:35: The Greek reads "from whatever day it comes into being, shall be its name," reflecting a different reading of the Hebrew consonants than the Masoretic Text's "The Lord Is There."
